messages.content: How does public key cryptography work?

Public key (asymmetric) cryptography uses a mathematically linked key pair: public key (sharable) and private key (secret). What is encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key. RSA example: Bob publishes his public key. Alice encrypts a message with Bob's public key. Only Bob's private key can decrypt it — even Alice cannot. The security rests on mathematical trapdoor functions: easy to compute in one direction, computationally infeasible to reverse without the private key. RSA trapdoor: multiplying two large primes is easy; factoring their product is computationally infeasible at sufficient key length. Digital signatures work in reverse: Bob signs with his private key; anyone with his public key can verify the signature is genuine.
How do password hashing algorithms work and how are they cracked?

Password hashing: one-way transformation of a password to a fixed-length hash for storage. Verification: hash the input, compare to stored hash — never store plaintext. Secure algorithms: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 — deliberately slow (10-1000ms per hash), computationally expensive, include salt (random per-user value preventing rainbow table attacks). Insecure: MD5, SHA-1 (fast, unsalted — crackers test billions per second). Cracking methods: dictionary attack (try common passwords + variants), brute force (all possible characters up to N length), rainbow tables (precomputed hash→password tables, defeated by salt), hybrid (dictionary + rules — capitalise, add numbers, substitute letters). Defence: Argon2id with sufficient memory factor is the current best practice — makes GPU cracking economically impractical.
What is AES encryption and why is it the global standard?

AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): symmetric block cipher adopted by NIST in 2001, now the global standard for symmetric encryption. Key sizes: 128, 192, or 256 bits. Block size: 128 bits. Operations: 10/12/14 rounds (depending on key size) of SubBytes (non-linear substitution), ShiftRows (transposition), MixColumns (linear transformation), and AddRoundKey (XOR with key material). Security: AES-256 with a random key has never been practically broken. Brute force: 2^256 possible keys — far beyond any foreseeable computational power. Side-channel attacks (timing, power analysis) are more practical than cryptanalysis. Modes of operation (CBC, GCM, CTR) matter greatly — AES in ECB mode is insecure even with strong keys.
What is the difference between encoding, encryption, and hashing?

Encoding: transforms data into a different format for compatibility — no secret involved. Base64 encodes binary as ASCII text. Anyone can decode it. Not security. Encryption: transforms data to ciphertext using a key — only someone with the decryption key can read it. Reversible with the key. Used for confidentiality. Hashing: one-way transformation — the hash cannot be reversed to the original input (in theory). Used for integrity verification and password storage. A hash of the same input always produces the same output. Even a single character change produces a completely different hash (avalanche effect). Common confusion: calling Base64 'encryption' — it is not. It provides no confidentiality. Only encryption with a strong key provides confidentiality.
How do you approach breaking a classical cipher?

Classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenere, Enigma) predate modern cryptography and rely on substitution or transposition. Attack methodology: (1) Frequency analysis — in English, 'e' is the most common letter (~13%), followed by 't', 'a', 'o', etc. In a substitution cipher, the most frequent ciphertext letter likely represents 'e'. (2) Index of Coincidence — measures whether ciphertext has natural language frequency distribution (substitution) or uniform distribution (transposition). (3) Kasiski examination — for polyalphabetic ciphers (Vigenere), finding repeated ciphertext sequences reveals key length. (4) Known plaintext — if you know part of the plaintext, the key can often be derived. Modern ciphertext is immune to these techniques — AES produces statistically uniform output regardless of input patterns.
